result: Enteroendocrine cells are specialized sensory cells of the gut-brain axis that are sparsely distributed along the intestinal epithelium, are electrically excitable, release vesicles upon calcium elevation, and form synaptic connections with second-order neurons through neuropods.
evaluation: Claims C1 and C7-C10 describe established knowledge about enteroendocrine cell properties, supported by citations to prior work (Gribble and Reimann, 2019; Bohórquez et al., 2015; Reimann et al., 2012). These are well-documented characteristics of enteroendocrine cells in the literature.

result: Individual enteroendocrine cells produce multiple gut hormones in combination, some gut hormones are produced elsewhere in the body, and single-cell RNA sequencing revealed five major enteroendocrine cell lineages defined by expression of GIP, ghrelin, serotonin, somatostatin, or a combination of GLP1, CCK, and/or neurotensin.
evaluation: Claims C2-C3 and C11-C12 are supported by citations to prior work (Lee and Soltesz, 2011; Okaty et al., 2019; Beumer et al., 2018; Gehart et al., 2019; Haber et al., 2017) and the manuscript's own transcriptomic data showing co-expression patterns. This establishes the complexity of enteroendocrine cell hormone production.

result: Vil1-p2a-FlpO knock-in mice restrict reporter expression to intestinal epithelium with high specificity, with expression throughout the entire length of the intestine and rare GFP-expressing cells in taste papillae, epiglottis, pancreas, liver, and thalamus.
evaluation: Claims C4 and C26-C29 are supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D, and citations to el Marjou et al., 2004; Maunoury et al., 1992; Höfer and Drenckhahn, 1999; Madison et al., 2002; Rutlin et al., 2020. The data demonstrate the specificity of the Vil1-p2a-FlpO allele for intestinal epithelium.

result: Combined use of Neurod1-Cre and Vil1-p2a-FlpO alleles (Neurod1INTER) yielded highly selective expression of an intersectional reporter gene in enteroendocrine cells, effectively targeting major transcriptome-defined enteroendocrine cell lineages.
evaluation: Claims C5 and C30 are supported by experimental data from two-color expression analysis and single-cell RNA sequencing shown in Figures 1C, 2, 3, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and E. The intersectional genetic strategy successfully restricts reporter expression to enteroendocrine cells with high selectivity.

result: Neurod1-Cre mice provide broad, indelible, and selective marking of enteroendocrine cells within the intestine, while Neurog3-Cre mice additionally label other intestinal cell types and neither Atoh1-Cre line tested displayed selective labeling of enteroendocrine cells. NeuroD1 is also expressed in brain, retina, pancreas, peripheral neurons, and enteric neurons, and its knockout is lethal.
evaluation: Claims C21-C25 are supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B, D, and E, and citations to Schonhoff et al., 2004; Cho and Tsai, 2004; Li et al., 2011; Gao et al., 2009; Naya et al., 1997. The data demonstrate the selectivity and limitations of different Cre lines for enteroendocrine cell labeling.

result: Twenty-five percent of Neurog3-lineage cells and 87% of NeuroD1-lineage cells expressed classical markers for enteroendocrine cells, with both Cre lines capturing the full diversity of known enteroendocrine cell types. NeuroD1 acts later than Neurogenin3 in the enteroendocrine cell lineage, but prior to cell fate decisions leading to enteroendocrine cell specialization.
evaluation: Claims C31-C35 are supported by experimental data from single-cell RNA sequencing shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C, and citation to Jenny et al., 2002. The data demonstrate that Neurod1-Cre provides more selective labeling of enteroendocrine cells compared to Neurog3-Cre, consistent with NeuroD1 acting later in the lineage.

result: Selective clustering analysis of 3049 enteroendocrine cells revealed 10 distinct cell clusters, including three classes of enterochromaffin cells that similarly express serotonin biosynthesis enzymes (Tph1) and associated transcription factors (Lmx1a), but differentially produce Tac1, Cartpt, Pyy, Ucn3, and Gad2. L, I, and N cells are thought to be derived from a common cell lineage.
evaluation: Claims C36-C38 are supported by experimental data from single-cell RNA sequencing shown in Figure 2A and B, and citations to Beumer et al., 2020; Gehart et al., 2019. The clustering analysis reveals the diversity of enteroendocrine cell types and subtypes.

result: Enteroendocrine cells detect sugars through the sodium-glucose cotransporter SGLT1 (Slc5a1), with expression highest in K, L, D, and N cells, while abundant expression of T1Rs was not detected in any enteroendocrine cell type. This is consistent with taste blind mice lacking T1Rs developing a preference for sugar-rich foods through SGLT1-mediated post-ingestive signals.
evaluation: Claims C39-C42 are supported by experimental data from single-cell RNA sequencing shown in Figure 2B and citations to Gorboulev et al., 2012; Reimann et al., 2008; Sclafani et al., 2016; Tan et al., 2020. The data demonstrate the mechanism of sugar detection by enteroendocrine cells.

result: Free fatty acid receptor genes Ffar1 and Ffar4 were broadly expressed in several enteroendocrine cell lineages but largely excluded from enterochromaffin cells, while the toxin receptor gene Trpa1 was enriched in enterochromaffin cells. Enterochromaffin cells also sense force through the mechanosensory ion channel PIEZO2.
evaluation: Claims C43-C45 are supported by experimental data from single-cell RNA sequencing shown in Figure 2B and D, and citations to Bellono et al., 2017; Alcaino et al., 2018; Billing et al., 2019; Treichel et al., 2022. The data demonstrate the differential expression of nutrient and toxin receptors across enteroendocrine cell types.

result: Seven intersectional combinations produced sparse labeling of intestinal epithelial cells, with striking selectivity for enteroendocrine cells observed for intersectional combinations targeting D, K, L, and I cells. Tac1INTER and Npy1rINTER alleles more broadly labeled rectal epithelium, and Npy1rINTER additionally labeled taste cells and rare cells in the airways and epiglottis.
evaluation: Claims C46-C49 are supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 1, 2, and 3B. The data demonstrate the selectivity and limitations of different intersectional genetic combinations for targeting enteroendocrine cell subtypes.

result: SstINTER mice showed enriched targeting of somatostatin cells throughout the intestine, while PetINTER driver captured cells with multiple hormones, suggesting that some enteroendocrine cells can transiently or durably express markers of multiple lineages or switch identity. GcgINTER mice labeled the majority of GLP1 cells.
evaluation: Claims C50-C52 are supported by experimental data from two-color expression analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4. The data demonstrate the selectivity of different intersectional genetic combinations and suggest plasticity in enteroendocrine cell identity.

result: PetINTER and SstINTER cells were most enriched in the duodenum and colon, GipINTER cells were enriched proximally with almost no cells in distal intestine, and GcgINTER cells were present along the entire proximal-distal axis and enriched in colon and rectum.
evaluation: Claims C53-C55 are supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3. The data demonstrate the distinct spatial distributions of different enteroendocrine cell subtypes along the gastrointestinal tract.

result: CNO-induced activation of enteroendocrine cells in Neurod1INTER; inter-hM3Dq-mCherry mice accelerated gut transit, while activation in all epithelial cells using Vil1-Cre; lsl-hM3Dq mice caused gavaged dye to fail to enter the intestine. CNO-accelerated gut transit was not observed in Ptf1aINTER; inter-hM3Dq-mCherry mice containing DREADD expression only in pancreatic cells, indicating the net effect of activating all enteroendocrine cells is to promote gut transit.
evaluation: Claims C57-C60 are supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B, and C. The data demonstrate that chemogenetic activation of enteroendocrine cells promotes gut transit, with appropriate controls ruling out effects from pancreatic cells.

result: Pet1INTER cells promoted gut transit, while SstINTER and GipINTER cells had no significant effect. Accelerated gut transit was observed upon chemogenetic activation of Tac1INTER cells but not Npy1rINTER cells, raising the possibility that each enterochromaffin cell subtype may privately communicate with different downstream neurons to control gut physiology.
evaluation: Claims C61-C63 are supported by experimental data from chemogenetic experiments shown in Figure 4. Claim C64 is speculation based on the differential effects observed, which is reasonable but requires further validation. The data demonstrate that different enteroendocrine cell subtypes have distinct effects on gut motility.

result: CckINTER and GcgINTER cells slowed gut motility, and simultaneous activation of both pathways in Neurod1INTER; inter-hM3Dq-mCherry mice masks the slowing of gut transit by these cells. This suggests a hierarchy where neural circuits that mediate toxin responses may achieve priority over those that mediate nutrient responses, at least under conditions of equal and maximal activation.
evaluation: Claim C65 is supported by experimental data from chemogenetic experiments shown in Figure 4. Claim C66 is speculation based on the experimental data, which is reasonable but requires further validation. The data demonstrate that different enteroendocrine cell subtypes have opposing effects on gut motility.

result: CNO-induced activation of enteroendocrine cells in Neurod1INTER; inter-hM3Dq-mCherry mice caused a 26% reduction in food intake. Chemogenetic activation of enterochromaffin cells reduced feeding behavior by 52.1%, while activation of SstINTER and GipINTER cells did not change feeding behavior. Activating GcgINTER cells reduced feeding by 52.4%, but activating CckINTER cells lowered feeding only in fed but not fasted mice.
evaluation: Claims C67-C71 are supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B. The data demonstrate that different enteroendocrine cell subtypes have distinct effects on feeding behavior, with some showing context-dependent effects.

result: Chemogenetic activation of GcgINTER cells caused a durable reduction of feeding for several hours with total food intake normalizing by 11 hr, and also evoked a decrease in water intake and the respiratory exchange ratio, but not locomotion. Activating somatostatin cells reduced the respiratory exchange ratio but did not change feeding, water intake, or locomotion.
evaluation: Claims C72-C74 are supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C. The data demonstrate the temporal dynamics and specificity of effects from activating different enteroendocrine cell subtypes on feeding and metabolic parameters.

result: Serotonin-producing enterochromaffin cells express the irritant receptor TRPA1 and chemogenetic activation blocks feeding behavior and promotes gut transit, presumably for toxin clearance. Different enterochromaffin cell subtypes can have different effects on gut motility, suggesting at least partially nonoverlapping communication pathways with downstream neurons. Pharmacological blockade of the serotonin receptor HTR3A is a clinical mainstay for nausea treatment.
evaluation: Claims C75, C77, and C78 are supported by citations to Bellono et al., 2017 and Freeman et al., 1992, and experimental data from chemogenetic experiments. Claim C76 is an inference based on experimental data, which is reasonable. The data and citations support the role of enterochromaffin cells in toxin-induced illness responses.

result: GLP1 cells slow gut motility, presumably to promote nutrient absorption and decrease feeding behavior.
evaluation: Claim C79 is supported by experimental data from chemogenetic experiments and citation to Gribble and Reimann, 2019. The inference about the functional role is reasonable based on the observed effects.

result: Chemogenetic activation of different enteroendocrine cell types variably impacted feeding behavior and gut motility.
evaluation: Claim C6 is a summary statement supported by experimental data from chemogenetic experiments shown in Figures 4 and 5. This is the main conclusion of the manuscript regarding the differential physiological effects of activating different enteroendocrine cell subtypes.

result: GLP1 and CCK are satiety hormones released following nutrient intake, ghrelin is an appetite-promoting hormone whose release is suppressed by nutrients, serotonin can be released by non-nutritive signals like irritants, force, and catecholamines, sugar-induced release of GIP and GLP1 causes the incretin effect which rapidly promotes insulin release and lowers blood glucose, and CCK, serotonin, and other gut hormones regulate various digestive functions.
evaluation: Claims C13-C17 describe established knowledge about gut hormone functions, supported by citation to Holst et al., 2009. These are well-documented characteristics of gut hormones in the literature.

result: Chemogenetic activation of enteroendocrine cells in the distal colon which express insulin-like peptide 5 triggers appetite suppression through a peptide YY (PYY) receptor, improved glucose tolerance through GLP1, and defecation indirectly through the serotonin receptor HTR3A.
evaluation: Claims C18-C20 are supported by citation to Lewis et al., 2020. This is prior work demonstrating the multipronged physiological response from activating a specific enteroendocrine cell population.

result: Neurogenin3 point mutations in human infants or intestine-targeted Neurog3 knockout cause loss of enteroendocrine cells, severe malabsorptive diarrhea, and increased mortality.
evaluation: Claim C56 is supported by citations to Mellitzer et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2006. This is prior work demonstrating the importance of enteroendocrine cells for intestinal function.
